attachments.origin_landmark: angle of the thyroid cartilage (the laryngeal cartilages are not modeled as skeletal elements in this pass -- approximated via the adjacent hyoid attachment region)
attachments.insertion_landmark: vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage and the vocal ligament

actions: makes fine local adjustments to the tension of individual parts of the vocal fold

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: The medial, deeper part of thyroarytenoid, lying within the vocal fold itself alongside the vocal ligament. Its fibres insert along the length of the ligament rather than only at its ends, which is what allows segmental rather than whole-fold tension change -- the basis of fine pitch control in singing.
functional_compartments.source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Moore KL, Dalley AF, Agur AMR, Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 8th ed.; Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Percutaneous EMG-guided injection through the cricothyroid membrane, not ultrasound: the same needle pass used for thyroarytenoid is used for vocalis, but directed slightly more medially/deeply so the tip lies within the medial, deeper part of the muscle complex immediately adjacent to the vocal ligament rather than in the bulk of the lateral thyroarytenoid; bilateral injection is typical.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Deep to the cricothyroid membrane, in the paraglottic space, at the medial margin of the thyroarytenoid complex adjacent to the vocal ligament -- the deepest part of the standard thyroarytenoid injection target.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: EMG activity increasing with phonation, as for thyroarytenoid; because vocalis and thyroarytenoid are not separately distinguishable by surface landmarks, correct depth (rather than a separate trajectory) is what differentiates a vocalis-weighted injection.
structures_at_risk: vocal ligament and mucosa -- overly medial/superficial placement risks submucosal injection and hematoma rather than intramuscular deposition
lateral cricoarytenoid and cricothyroid muscles, which can receive diffusion as they do from a thyroarytenoid injection generally
contralateral vocal fold, if the needle crosses the midline
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Vocalis is the medial, deep part of thyroarytenoid and is not injected as an anatomically separate target in routine adductor spasmodic dysphonia treatment; it is nonetheless the specific target named in some indications, e.g. bilateral percutaneous vocalis injection described for essential/action voice tremor. Guidance is by EMG, never ultrasound.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Blitzer A, Brin MF, Stewart CF, 'Botulinum toxin management of spasmodic dysphonia (laryngeal dystonia): a 12-year experience in more than 900 patients', Laryngoscope 108(10):1435-1441 (1998), doi:10.1097/00005537-199810000-00003 (https://doi.org/10.1097/00005537-199810000-00003); Warrick P, Dromey C, Irish J, Durkin L, 'The treatment of essential voice tremor with botulinum toxin A: a longitudinal case report', J Voice 14(3):410-421 (2000), doi:10.1016/s0892-1997(00)80086-7 (https://doi.org/10.1016/s0892-1997(00)80086-7) -- percutaneous bilateral vocalis injection; Lee HJ, Kim IB, Kim BH, Lee JH, 'Analysis of Dye Distribution in Cadaveric Supraglottic Injections...', J Voice (2026), doi:10.1016/j.jvoice.2026.04.016 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jvoice.2026.04.016) -- all retrieved via PubMed
